name: CRA Bureau
tagline: Web tooling for consumer credit report work: intake, dispute letter generation against the reporting bureaus, and outcome tracking.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The visible surface is unglamorous CRUD: contacts, report items, letters, dates, statuses, and an agent will happily generate all of it in an afternoon. The part that matters is everything touching the consumer reporting agencies, which is gated by contracts, identity verification, permissible purpose, and a stack of regulation you do not get to route around with an API key. Anything that generates dispute correspondence on someone's behalf also lands near FCRA and credit repair rules, which is a bad place to be clever alone. A personal build is defensible only if you are working your own file and typing the report data in by hand. As a business tool it does not survive the loss of the data pipes and the paperwork.
coreLoopDIY: A local tracker where you hand-enter report items, generate dispute letters from templates, and watch the response clocks tick.
requirements: your own credit reports, pulled manually
whatYouLose: Any direct connection to bureau or data-furnisher systems; everything becomes manual typing
Compliance framing: disclosures, retention rules, and the paperwork that keeps regulated work defensible
Mail handling, certified send, proof of delivery, and the audit trail that goes with it
Multi-client operations: staff roles, client portals, billing, and the reporting a business actually runs on
Whoever wrote the letter templates knows what language works; yours will be guesses
moatNotes: Access to consumer report data is a contractual and legal privilege, not an integration task.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the app is the boring wrapper around permissions you cannot self-grant. Paying gets a pipeline to report data, letter language that has survived contact with actual bureaus and furnishers, and a record of who did what and when that holds up if someone asks. Rebuilding the forms is trivial; rebuilding the position that makes the forms legal is not. For anyone doing this at volume, the subscription is cheaper than one compliance mistake.
notes: The letter generator and the date math are a weekend, and neither is the product. The moat is permissible access to bureau data plus the regulatory posture that lets you act on it.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user credit report dispute tracker. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db, migrations in plain SQL on boot
- PDF letters rendered server side with pdf-lib
- Runs with: npm install && npm run dev on localhost only

Data model:
- report_pull: bureau (equifax | experian | transunion), pulled_on, notes
- item: report_pull_id, furnisher_name, account_ref, item_type (account | inquiry | public_record | personal_info), claim (what is wrong), status (open | disputed | verified | deleted | corrected)
- dispute: item_id, bureau, sent_on, method (mail | certified | online), expected_response_by (sent_on + 30 days), response_on, outcome, evidence_notes
- event log: append only, every insert and status change, timestamped, never editable

Features, in scope:
- Manual entry and CSV import of items; I type in what my own reports say, there is no bureau connection
- Letter builder: pick items, pick a Markdown template from ./templates, mail merge my details from .env, render a dated PDF to ./out
- Dashboard: open items, disputes awaiting response, anything past expected_response_by, sorted by urgency
- Timeline view per furnisher showing every dispute and outcome
- Full JSON export and a one file SQLite backup command

Explicitly out of scope, do not fake these:
- Any bureau, furnisher, or credit data API
- Identity verification, e-signature, certified mail integration, payments, client portals, multi tenancy
- Legal advice, auto generated legal claims, or templates that assert facts I did not enter

Templates ship as three neutral examples with placeholders and a README line saying I am responsible for the wording.
Secrets and personal details (name, address, file numbers) live in .env, never committed, and .gitignore covers .env, ./data, ./out.
Write a README with setup, the data model, and a short honest note that this is a personal recordkeeping tool, not a compliance system.
